clue.text: The river, love, is some distance for tea

parts.note: the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the letter O
a mile is a measure of distance

explanation.surface: A riverside picnic where someone muses on how far they must go for a cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The river' in crosswords is often the Cam, Cambridge's river. The tea meant is the herbal infusion made from the plant's flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a daisy-like plant whose dried flowers are brewed as a herbal infusion.

parts.note: a con is a swindle, so swindling gives this short word
firms are businesses

explanation.surface: Fraudulent companies set themselves up, a sly comment on dodgy trade.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm something is to establish it as true or settled.

clue.text: Shows how a feint's' involved in written matter

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed in the abbreviation for written matter

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, written matter

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so the letters of a feint's are jumbled

explanation.surface: An explanation of how a feint is worked into a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how' is only a link. The anagram of A FEINTS, ANIFEST, goes 'in' MS.
explanation.definitionFit: To manifest something is to display it plainly, to show it.

definitions.meaning: a musical key can be major or this sort
being given the key of the door marks coming of age at 21, so someone not given it is underage

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 21st birthday was celebrated as getting 'the key of the door', so someone without it is still a child in law.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical key may be this, and an underage person, not yet given the key of the door, is one too.

indicators.note: ambience suggests the letters of rose-lit are surrounded by a fresh setting and so rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lingers in a pink, softly lit atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ambience' is the anagram signal working on ROSE-LIT; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To dawdle about idly is to linger without purpose.

clue.text: Gas-burner produces cake on the old side

parts.note: a bun is a small sweet cake
Sen. is the abbreviation of senior, someone older than another

explanation.surface: A kitchen remark that a gas ring is turning out cakes that are a bit stale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produces' is only a link. Sen., short for senior, as in 'John Smith Sen.', marks the older of two people with one name, so the one 'on the old side'.
explanation.definitionFit: This laboratory burner, named after the chemist who popularised it, mixes gas and air for a hot flame.

clue.text: Lucy's ways beside the springs of Dove

definitions.text: Lucy's ways beside the springs of Dove

parts.words: Lucy's ways beside the springs of Dove
parts.note: Wordsworth's Lucy poem begins 'She dwelt among the ... ways / Beside the springs of Dove'

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue from Wordsworth's 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways', one of his Lucy poems; Dove is an English river.
explanation.definitionFit: The ways in Wordsworth's poem are paths that no feet have walked.

parts.note: so means thus, in that way
USA is the abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A patriotic image of the United States marching on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the composer known as the March King, whose marches include 'The Stars and Stripes Forever'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa was an American composer famed for his military marches.

clue.text: Pinched a projection over the couch

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places one piece above the next

parts.note: a nab is a projecting part, such as a rocky headland or the catch of a lock
a bed is a couch to lie on

explanation.surface: Someone describes a ledge jutting out above a sofa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' means stolen or arrested, not squeezed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabbed is slang for caught or stolen, both senses of pinched.

indicators.note: a portrait is a drawing, so the letters of crayon are redrawn in a new order

explanation.surface: A crayon drawing made by the French playwright Rostand.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmond Rostand wrote 'Cyrano de Bergerac', so the definition is 'Rostand's' hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostand's best-known play has a long-nosed swordsman-poet as its hero.

clue.text: Tontine arranged in New York for Mr. Pooter ?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed inside the abbreviation for the American city
arranged signals that the letters of the word tontine are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a tontine investment scheme in New York for a Victorian clerk.
explanation.walkthrough: A tontine is an old annuity scheme in which the last surviving subscriber takes all. Mr Pooter is the hero of 'The Diary of a Nobody' by George and Weedon Grossmith.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Pooter is the self-important clerk of 'The Diary of a Nobody', the title making him a person of no importance.

parts.note: Little Jack Horner in the nursery rhyme put in a digit and pulled out a plum, lifting it; a hitch-hiker's raised digit also signals that a lift is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Two pictures meet here: the nursery-rhyme boy who 'put in his thumb and pulled out a plum', and the hitch-hiker's gesture asking drivers for a ride.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the digit that Little Jack Horner used to lift out his plum and that hitch-hikers raise when asking for a ride.

clue.text: Conclude one might be soundly pelted ?

indicators.note: soundly tells us the words for being pelted are to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: pelted here means wearing pelts, that is clad in fur

explanation.surface: Someone decides they might be pelted with missiles, and thoroughly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pelted' looks like being bombarded, but it means wearing pelts: 'in fur', which said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce something is to reach a conclusion from evidence.

clue.text: To be a real turn, it must be worked out in detail

indicators.note: a turn here is a twist or change of order applied to the preceding letters

explanation.surface: A verdict that a stage act, to be genuine, needs careful planning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' looks like a music-hall act, but it signals that TO BE A REAL is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something planned with great care and intricacy is intricate in every particular.

clue.text: They prepare the Murphies to be Lady-killers

definitions.meaning: Murphies is old slang for potatoes, and kitchen tools crush cooked potatoes smooth
a masher was an Edwardian dandy who pursued women

explanation.walkthrough: 'Murphies', from the Irish surname, is old slang for potatoes; the second sense is the Victorian and Edwardian word for a fashionable flirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitchen implements pulp boiled potatoes, and in old slang the same word meant dandies who chased women.

parts.note: read as a noun, a being made wholly of spirit, a nature spirit of earth, air, fire or water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a verb and 'full of spirit' like lively, but the clue describes a supernatural creature.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore and the occult, a nature spirit associated with one of the four classical elements bears this name.

parts.note: when several people toss coins, the one whose coin differs from the rest is eliminated

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is completed by 'out': in a coin-tossing elimination, the player whose result is unlike the others' drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: In the game 'odd man out' the player whose tossed coin differs from everyone else's is excluded.

parts.note: the proverb says charity begins at home; a charitable institution once housed the poor

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'charity begins at home' is turned around: a home run by charity is the place.
explanation.definitionFit: Charitable foundations built houses where poor and elderly people lived free of rent.

parts.note: court plaster was an old adhesive dressing of silk, so courtly stickers are adhesive dressings

explanation.walkthrough: Court plaster, silk coated with isinglass, was used for beauty patches by court ladies and later for small cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesive dressings for cuts, once called court plaster, stick to the skin.

clue.text: Blokes 'oo get you seated and keep you quiet?

definitions.meaning: attendants in a theatre or church who show people to their seats
said in Cockney with the h dropped, as 'oo for who shows, hushers are people who silence you

explanation.walkthrough: The dropped h in 'oo (who) tells you to drop the h from hushers too; that gives the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Attendants show audiences to their seats, and with a Cockney dropped h the same word names people who hush you.

parts.note: Lewis Carroll wrote a two-volume novel about a fairy girl and her brother Bruno

explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's late novel 'Sylvie and Bruno' names the brother; the answer is his sister.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lewis Carroll's novel the fairy children are a girl and her little brother Bruno.

clue.text: Small car no good abroad, to say the least

parts.note: the Mini is a famous small British car
mal is French for bad, so no good in a foreign tongue

explanation.surface: A traveller finds that a little car is useless overseas, putting it mildly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something minimal is the smallest possible amount, the least that could be said or done.

definitions.meaning: a small French bagpipe of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries
a muse is a source of inspiration, and the ending -ette makes a little one

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word as MUSE + the diminutive ending -ETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small French bagpipe, and read as muse plus the diminutive ending it means a small source of inspiration.

definitions.meaning: Samuel ... was the Victorian author of 'Self-Help'

explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Smiles was a Scottish writer whose 'Self-Help' (1859) preached self-improvement.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Smiles was a Victorian advocate of self-improvement, and grins are what a beaming face shows.

parts.note: 24 refers to the answer at 24-down, a citizen of Rome; the platform is the battlements at Elsinore where the ghost appears in Hamlet

explanation.walkthrough: 24 is 24-down, ROMAN. One of the officers on watch on the battlements of Elsinore in the opening scene of Shakespeare's Hamlet has a Roman name, also borne by a famous Roman general.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer who sees the ghost on the castle battlements in Hamlet bears the name of a Roman general.

definitions.meaning: a citizen of Rome, the Italian capital
upright typeface, as opposed to italic

explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Rome comes from the capital, and upright print is the type used for most text.

indicators.note: bad signals that the letters of the word shot are in a poor or disordered state

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to believe that a skilled marksman could miss.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: one of Dumas's Three Musketeers could never be a poor shot, so 'Impossible!' answers the question.
explanation.definitionFit: Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, a swordsman and marksman who would not miss.

clue.text: "When I shall voice -how good He is " (Lovelace)

definitions.text: When I shall voice -how good He is

parts.words: When I shall voice -how good He is
parts.note: the gap is filled from Lovelace's 'To Althea, from Prison': 'When I shall voice ... how good / He is'

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue from Richard Lovelace's poem 'To Althea, from Prison'; the missing word means out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice something out loud is to speak it so others can hear.

clue.text: Sign illuminated at both ends of the motorway

indicators.note: the word for illuminated sits at both ends, so it wraps around the road

parts.note: something illuminated is lit up
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written here as MI

explanation.surface: A road sign lit up at either end of the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Yorkshire; its 1 is read as the letter I. The definition is the road sign posting a speed restriction.
explanation.definitionFit: A speed restriction is posted on a road sign, so the word names that kind of sign.

clue.text: Credit UNO with capacity to bring people together

indicators.note: the letters of credit uno are given the capacity to change into another word, an unusual anagram signal

explanation.surface: A tribute to the United Nations for its power to bring nations together.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is 'with capacity': the letters of CREDIT UNO have the capacity to be rearranged. UNO is the United Nations Organization.
explanation.definitionFit: To present one person to another by name is to make them acquainted.

parts.note: the gap is filled by the word that opens Wordsworth's 'The Solitary Reaper': 'Behold her, ... in the field, / Yon solitary Highland Lass'

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the missing word comes from the first line of Wordsworth's poem 'The Solitary Reaper', meaning alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland girl in Wordsworth's poem reaps alone, one by herself in the field.

clue.text: Not caring, he had not so much, 'tis said

indicators.note: 'tis said means the phrase is spoken, so its sound gives the answer

parts.note: he'd less, a contraction of he had less, means he had not so much

explanation.surface: A remark that someone careless had less than others, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he had not so much' is HE'D LESS, which said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone heedless pays no attention, careless of warnings or consequences.
